title: Can GPS be used to detect deleterious progression in training volume among runners?
authors: Nielsen RO, Cederholm P, Buist I, Sorensen H, Lind M, Rasmussen S
journal: Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research
population: 60 novice runners in a 10-week prospective study with GPS volume tracking and clinical examination of injuries
findings: 60 novice runners over 10 weeks; 13 sustained an injury.
The injured runners had a significantly higher weekly progression in total training volume in the week before injury origin than in other weeks (86%, 95% CI 12.9-159.9, p=0.026).
Participants with injuries had a weekly volume increase of 31.6% versus 22.1% among healthy participants, which was not significant.
GPS volume measurement error was 6.2% or less in open landscape, forest and urban areas.

Authors say weekly increases may become deleterious above 30% (more than the 10% rule), that no clear evidence for safe progression exists, and that some individuals may tolerate 20-25% for a short time.
limitations: Very small sample with few injuries; within-person comparison of the week before injury with other weeks; the authors' 30% figure is an interpretation, not a tested cut-off. Abstract-level verification only. Different paper from nielsen-2014-weekly-progression and nielsen-2013-novice-predictors in the corpus.
implications: Supports a hard weekly ramp ceiling nearer 30% than 10% for novices, with the 10% a conservative default and 20-25% described as tolerable for some people only; grade C/D.
The healthy novices averaged a 22.1% weekly increase without injury, so a strict 10% novice rule has no support in this study.
